design_detail: President's Address to the newly founded Section of Occupational Medicine of the Royal Society of Medicine, meeting of 14 January 1965, printed in the Proceedings (6 pages, 7 references; single author, Sir Austin Bradford Hill, Professor Emeritus of Medical Statistics, University of London). Hill asks which aspects of an association, clear-cut and beyond what would be attributed to chance, should be considered before deciding that causation is its most likely interpretation, and lists nine 'viewpoints': strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment and analogy, each illustrated with examples from occupational and smoking epidemiology, several from his own work, and each followed by its limits. He then argues that tests of significance cannot answer the causal question and are overused, and that the strength of evidence required before acting can depend on what the action would cost. No new data, no search and no quantitative synthesis: an expert lecture, filed as a narrative review and appraised with the editors' narrative-review checklist.
can_establish: What Hill himself argued: which features of an association make a causal reading more or less likely, that none of them is decisive or required, what significance tests can and cannot show, and why absolute and relative differences answer different questions.
cannot_establish: Whether any particular association, including a drug's link to a harm, is causal: the viewpoints are judgements, not a validated scoring rule, and the epidemiological figures in the lecture are illustrations taken from other reports and Hill's own earlier work, given without methods.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (lecture). Examples: Pott's chimney sweeps, with Doll's figure of scrotal cancer mortality some 200 times that of unexposed workers (as quoted, p. 295); prospective studies of smoking and lung cancer, including death rates by amount smoked in doctors (p. 296); Snow's analysis of the 1854 cholera epidemic (p. 296); the 1964 report of the Advisory Committee to the US Surgeon-General (pp. 296, 298); Heady's (1958) hospital controls (p. 296); nickel refiners in South Wales, from Hill's 1962 lecture and later figures by Doll (p. 297); and Hill's 1930 study of sickness in Lancashire cotton mills (p. 299).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; examples chosen by the speaker.
sample.selection_effects: The worked examples are mostly associations Hill presents as causal (smoking and lung cancer, nickel refining, chimney soot, polluted water); the counter-examples are a weaker association more open to confounding (smoking and coronary thrombosis) and a bias that every repetition of the same design reproduces (Heady's hospital controls) (p. 296). Several examples come from Hill's own studies.

comparison.controls: Not applicable. In the examples the comparisons are non-smokers, workers not specially exposed, houses supplied by a rival water company, deaths expected from national rates, and patients admitted for hernia as controls for patients admitted for peptic ulcer.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. Under temporality Hill asks whether early disease leads to the behaviour rather than the reverse, and whether people who choose an occupation are already ill, or more liable to the disease, whatever the environment (pp. 297–298).

outcomes.operationalization: Causation is framed practically: whether the frequency of an undesirable event B would be influenced by a change in the environmental feature A; the mechanism may need much research, but action need not always wait for it (p. 295).

analysis.effect_sizes: Not applicable (no synthesis). Figures used as illustrations: lung cancer death rates of 0.07 per 1,000 per year in non-smoking doctors against 0.57, 1.39 and 2.27 in those smoking 1–14, 15–24 and 25 or more cigarettes a day, ratios of 8, 20 and 32 to 1 (p. 296; editors' calculation: absolute differences of 0.50, 1.32 and 2.20 deaths per 1,000 per year); lung cancer death rate in cigarette smokers nine to ten times that of non-smokers and twenty to thirty times in heavy smokers, coronary thrombosis no more than twice (pp. 295–296); cholera deaths of 71 against 5 per 10,000 houses, 14 times (p. 296); the smoking–lung cancer association found in 29 retrospective and 7 prospective inquiries (p. 296); nickel refiners (about one thousand at risk), 1929–1938: 16 lung cancer deaths against about one expected and 11 nasal sinus cancer deaths against a fraction of one; 1948–1956: 48 and 13 against 10 and 0.1 expected (p. 297); other causes of death raised 10, 20 or even 50% in smokers against 900–1,000% for lung cancer (p. 297); cardroom workers aged 30 to 60 had over three times as much respiratory sickness as other operatives and no difference in other sickness (p. 299).

interpretation_gap.results_show: An argued list of nine features to weigh before calling an association causal, each with its limits, and an argument that significance tests speak only to chance.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Hill himself states that none of the nine viewpoints can bring indisputable evidence for or against cause and effect and none can be required as a sine qua non, and he rejects hard-and-fast rules of evidence (p. 299). The gap lies in later use, not in the lecture: sources on file treat the viewpoints as 'criteria' to be met — a systematic review judged take-home naloxone against the nine Bradford Hill criteria (card sc_mcdonald_2016), and the GBD 2016 alcohol analysis modelled only outcomes it judged causal by them (as recorded in the project's checks of sc_griswold_2018).

timeline.event: Snow's analysis of deaths in the 1854 cholera epidemic by water company (as cited, p. 296).
Heady's example of hospital controls who are not comparable with the cases (as cited, p. 296).
Hill's Alfred Watson Memorial Lecture on the South Wales nickel refiners (as quoted, pp. 297–298).

Report of the Advisory Committee to the US Surgeon-General on smoking: the lung cancer association in 29 retrospective and 7 prospective inquiries, and 'coherence' as one of its considerations (as cited, pp. 296, 298).
McDonald and Strang judge take-home naloxone programmes against the nine Bradford Hill criteria (card sc_mcdonald_2016).
The GBD 2016 alcohol analysis chooses the outcomes it models by Bradford Hill criteria (as recorded in the project's checks of sc_griswold_2018).

replication.where_it_stands: The lecture is the source of what are now called the Bradford Hill criteria. Hill offered them as viewpoints to weigh, explicitly not as rules or requirements; claims citing him should keep that framing, and the figures in the lecture should be cited from their primary sources. For the site's 'Seven questions': it bears on question 1 (non-comparable hospital controls; samples losing an unknown share of people), question 2 (temporality: which came first, and who chose the exposure; confounding of weak associations), question 4 (significance tests address chance only; 'not significant' is not 'no difference'), question 5 (with a difference: absolute differences answer how many extra cases, ratios are more informative for judging causation), question 6 (consistency, with the limits that repeating a biased design repeats its bias and that one unrepeatable study can sometimes suffice) and, throughout, 'linked to is not causes'. Its dose–response viewpoint concerns how risk changes with amount, not laboratory doses against daily use (question 3), and it does not discuss summaries or headlines (question 7).

funding.funder: Not reported (presidential address to a section of the Royal Society of Medicine).
funding.affiliations_note: Professor Emeritus of Medical Statistics, University of London (p. 295). Several examples are from Hill's own work: the prospective study of doctors' smoking with Doll (Doll & Hill, 1964, in the reference list), his 1930 study of Lancashire cotton-mill workers for the Industrial Health Research Board of the Medical Research Council, and his 1962 lecture (pp. 296–300).

what_would_settle_it: Not applicable to an argument. Whether the viewpoints sort causal from non-causal associations well could be tested only against a set of associations whose causal status was later settled by experiment or natural experiment.

domains.note: A lecture; examples chosen by the speaker; no search.

Biases are discussed as principles (non-comparable hospital controls, p. 296; volunteers, losses to follow-up and people never contacted, p. 299), but the illustrative figures come without methods, and the doctors' death rates are not attributed in the text.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The smoking, nickel and cotton-mill examples draw on Hill's own work; the argument itself does not depend on them.
The viewpoints are offered as judgements with their limits stated; Hill flags his own exaggeration about significance tests (p. 299).

domains.domain: Balance of arguments for and against each viewpoint (worked examples of associations that met several viewpoints yet proved non-causal are few)
domains.note: Each viewpoint is followed by its 'obverse' (strength, consistency, specificity, plausibility, coherence); the counter-examples are a weak, easily confounded association and a bias that repetition reproduces (p. 296).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to an expert lecture (METHODS §5.3). The overall 'high' follows the rule that it can be no milder than the worst domain and reflects only the absence of a search. Cite the lecture for Hill's own arguments: the nine viewpoints, none decisive or required; significance tests address chance only and 'no significant difference' is not 'no difference'; absolute and relative differences answer different questions; action may be taken on incomplete evidence, with stronger evidence required when more is at stake. Cite its epidemiological figures as his illustrations, and from their primary sources if used as evidence.

key_findings.finding: The question Hill poses: given an association between two variables that is clear-cut and beyond what one would attribute to chance, which aspects should be considered before deciding that causation is its most likely interpretation; for preventive medicine, the decisive question is whether the frequency of an outcome would change if the environmental feature changed.

Strength: a large ratio is harder to explain away. The lung cancer death rate in cigarette smokers was nine to ten times that of non-smokers, and twenty to thirty times in heavy smokers, whereas the coronary thrombosis death rate in smokers was no more than twice, possibly less, that of non-smokers; for the weaker association it is much easier to imagine features of life going with smoking (lack of exercise, diet) as the real cause or an important contributor. Hill adds that a weak association should not be dismissed for that reason alone.
key_findings.locator: (1) Strength, 2nd paragraph (p. 295, right column, continuing on p. 296) and 5th paragraph (p. 296)
key_findings.note: Bears on 'linked to is not causes' and on the site's question 2: weaker associations are more open to confounding.

key_findings.finding: Absolute versus relative: to know how many extra lung cancer deaths smoking causes, presuming causation, the absolute differences in death rates are needed (per 1,000 per year: 0.07 in non-smoking doctors; 0.57, 1.39 and 2.27 at 1–14, 15–24 and 25 or more cigarettes a day); for judging causation the ratios (8, 20 and 32 to 1) are more informative; and the ratios do not by themselves show that a difference matters in practice. Snow's cholera figures make the same point: 71 deaths per 10,000 houses supplied with polluted water is a low rate, but 14 times the 5 per 10,000 in houses with clean water.
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's question 5 (out of how many?) with a difference: Hill rejects the view that only absolute differences matter and gives each measure its own question. The text layer garbles the decimal points of the death rates; read them on the rendered page. Editors' calculation: absolute differences of 0.50, 1.32 and 2.20 deaths per 1,000 per year.

key_findings.finding: Consistency: whether the association has been observed repeatedly by different persons, in different places, circumstances and times; some associations found in industry will pass the customary tests of significance, yet whether chance or a true hazard explains them may sometimes be answered only by repeating the circumstances and observations; the US Surgeon-General's Advisory Committee found the smoking–lung cancer association in 29 retrospective and 7 prospective inquiries.
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's question 6 ('Did another team find the same?').

key_findings.finding: Repetition has limits: a bias built into a design is neither removed nor revealed by repeating it (Heady's example: patients admitted for peptic ulcer operations, asked about recent crises, against hernia patients, who can choose when to come in); the same results from exactly the same form of inquiry do not always add much, while similar results reached in quite different ways (prospectively and retrospectively) carry weight; conversely, a unique observation that cannot be repeated can be convincing (the nickel refiners).
key_findings.note: Where Hill says more than the site's question 6: one study can sometimes suffice, and many studies with the same design can share the same error.

key_findings.finding: Nickel refiners in South Wales (quoted from Hill's 1962 lecture; about one thousand workers and pensioners at risk): in 1929–1938, 16 deaths from lung cancer against about one expected and 11 from nasal sinus cancer against a fraction of one, while other cancers (11 against 10–11 expected) and other causes (67 against 72) were not raised; in 1948–1956, 48 lung and 13 nasal cancer deaths against 10 and 0.1 expected (Doll's figures); no nasal cancer and no lung cancer excess in men who first entered the works after changes made in 1923.
key_findings.locator: (2) Consistency, 6th paragraph and the quoted passage that follows it
key_findings.note: Hill's illustration of a conclusion drawn without repetition, and of specificity; the figures are second-hand.

key_findings.finding: Specificity counts in favour of causation when present but should not be over-emphasized: diseases can have more than one cause and one agent can cause several diseases; when other causes of death are raised 10, 20 or even 50% in smokers but lung cancer 900–1,000%, the specificity lies in the size of the association; if specificity is absent, no conclusion follows from its absence.

Temporality: which comes first, exposure or disease. Does a particular diet lead to disease, or do the early stages of the disease lead to the diet? Does an occupation promote tuberculosis, or are the people who select that work more liable to it, or already infected? To be remembered particularly where selective factors are at work.
key_findings.locator: (4) Temporality, 1st paragraph (p. 297, right column, continuing on p. 298)
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's question 2 ('Were they tested before they started?'): reverse causation and self-selection, in Hill's examples.

key_findings.finding: Biological gradient: a dose–response curve, such as lung cancer death rates rising linearly with the number of cigarettes smoked a day, adds a very great deal to the case; a higher death rate in light than in heavy smokers would weaken it; the difficulty is often a satisfactory measure of exposure, but it should always be sought.
key_findings.note: Related to the site's question 3 ('How much, how often, and how?') only through the emphasis on amount; Hill says nothing about laboratory doses against everyday use.

key_findings.finding: Plausibility and coherence: biological plausibility helps but cannot be demanded, since it depends on the knowledge of the day; a causal reading should not seriously conflict with the generally known natural history and biology of the disease; laboratory evidence can greatly strengthen a hypothesis, but its absence cannot nullify observations in people (arsenic causes skin cancer in man, though this had never been shown in another animal).
Experiment: the strongest support for causation may come when preventive action is taken (dust reduced, oils changed, people stop smoking) and the frequency of the associated events changes.
key_findings.locator: (8) Experiment, 1st paragraph (p. 298, right column, continuing on p. 299)

key_findings.finding: None of the nine viewpoints can bring indisputable evidence for or against cause and effect, and none can be required as a sine qua non; Hill does not believe in hard-and-fast rules of evidence; what the viewpoints do is help answer whether any other explanation of the facts is equally or more likely than cause and effect.
key_findings.locator: Paragraph after (9) Analogy, beginning 'Here then are nine different viewpoints'
key_findings.note: Bears on 'linked to is not causes'. Later sources call these 'criteria' to be met (see interpretation_gap).

key_findings.finding: Significance tests cannot answer the causal question: they remind us of the effects that chance can create and of their likely size, and beyond that contribute nothing to proof. In Hill's 1930 cotton-mill study (cardroom workers aged 30 to 60 had over three times as much respiratory sickness as other operatives, set out in 36 tables) no test was used because the differences were so large and specific.
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's question 4 ('How big is the difference?').

key_findings.finding: Hill grants that significance tests were a useful corrective when conclusions were drawn from very small numbers, but argues that the pendulum has swung too far: tests are often unnecessary because a difference is grotesquely obvious, negligible, or, significant or not, too small to be of practical importance; their glitter can divert attention from flaws in the sample (an unknown fraction volunteering, 20% of patients lost to sight, 30% of a random sample never contacted, given as examples); and far too often 'no difference' is deduced from 'no significant difference'.
key_findings.locator: Tests of Significance, 4th–6th paragraphs (p. 299, right column, the 6th continuing on p. 300)
key_findings.note: Bears on the site's question 4: a significant difference can be too small to matter, and Hill adds the converse error, that 'not significant' is not 'no difference'.

key_findings.finding: Case for action: on scientific grounds the judgement of the evidence should be independent of what follows from it, but in practice the evidence required before acting can differ with the consequences — relatively slight evidence to restrict a drug for morning sickness in pregnancy, fair evidence to change an industrial oil, very strong evidence to make people change their fuel, stop smoking or change their diet; all scientific work is incomplete and liable to be modified, but that does not justify ignoring current knowledge or postponing the action it appears to demand.

reporting_issues.issue: The doctors' lung cancer death rates (0.07 to 2.27 per 1,000 per year) and the coronary thrombosis comparison are given without a source in the text; the reference list includes Doll and Hill (1964) and the 1964 Surgeon-General's report.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the primary source for these figures, not the lecture.

reporting_issues.issue: The lung cancer rate in smokers is given as nine to ten times that of non-smokers (p. 295) and later as raised 900–1,000% (p. 297), so the two figures do not match exactly (editors' calculation: a nine- to ten-fold rate is a rise of 800–900%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: Hill's point (specificity in the size of the association) is unchanged; a claim using the smoking figure should give the ratio as printed on p. 295.
